title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
body: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It An AI-defined fab uses accelerated simulation, learned physics models and AI agents to give engineers faster answers across design, testing and manufacturing. November 3, 2026 by Timothy Costa 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers. Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing. Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress. Using the NVIDIA cuDSS library, multiphysics software provider COMSOL is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically. Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster. In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating NVIDIA cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print. As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes. Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time. The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware. Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time. Applied Materials uses digital twins built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to simulate fab-level optimizations in layout, throughput, cost and process control. Agents Handle the Steps Between Decisions Engineers turn analyses into decisions — revising a design, investigating a test failure, adjusting a production process and more. AI agents can help carry out the steps between those decisions. Evaluating which AI model to apply to a given task is one example: a sequential, manual process that can consume hours on the test floor. Advantest is using NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate that selection, reducing response times from hours to minutes. Testing Factory Changes Before They Reach the Line Digital twins let teams simulate equipment configurations, layouts and process changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. This reduces experimentation costs, especially as fabs become more complex and the stakes of a wrong change get higher. A photorealistic fab digital twin built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, used to simulate material flow, spot bottlenecks and validate operational strategies before deployment. Image courtesy of Applied Materials. Applied Materials uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabs. Teams can simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and evaluate layouts and operating strategies — extending virtual experimentation beyond individual processes to how the factory works as a whole. The Connected Loop The future of semiconductor manufacturing lies in connecting these capabilities: using production data to inform models and models to evaluate changes, then bringing those findings back to the engineers making production decisions. That’s the promise of the AI-defined fab: where AI helps people learn from each production cycle and act on that knowledge sooner. Explore how NVIDIA is working with semiconductor leaders across the chip lifecycle. body: New research shows how Guided Learning supports students Nov 03, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Two new studies show how Guided Learning boosts student performance, plus new Google Classroom features that give teachers more control. Sofie Cornelis Senior Product Manager, Google for Education Asha Johnson Product Manager, Google DeepMind Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. New research shows this approach leads to higher learning gains and allows teachers to provide more targeted support. You can now use these tools in your classroom to assign guided lessons, track student progress, and gain insights into how your students interact with course materials. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are rolling out Guided Learning in Google Classroom to help students master complex academic concepts. Research shows students using Guided Learning achieved significantly higher test scores than those using standard tools. Teachers can now assign specific course materials to guide students through lessons with step-by-step support. Our new educator insights allow teachers to track student progress and provide targeted help when needed. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are rolling out Guided Learning in Google Classroom to help students master difficult topics step by step. Instead of giving direct answers, this tool coaches students through complex concepts, practice quizzes, and custom visual aids. Research shows this approach helps students learn more effectively during independent study. Teachers can now assign these guided lessons, track student progress, and spend more time providing one-on-one support where it is needed most. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer We’re sharing two new studies that show how Guided Learning supports students and teachers in real-world settings. Alongside these findings, today we’re starting to roll out Guided Learning in Google Classroom , giving teachers even more control over how and when this tool is used in their classrooms. Guided Learning is designed to help students work through complex concepts step by step, prioritizing deep understanding over providing direct answers. Boosting statistics scores To see how Guided Learning impacts real performance, we conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with more than 300 students at the University of Tokyo. We wanted to test whether Guided Learning provided extra value beyond standard study tools. All students were given half a day to independently study a statistics lesson using standard online resources. Half of the group was also given access to Guided Learning in the Gemini app. Instead of looking for quick answers, students used Guided Learning to dig deeper. They frequently asked for practice quizzes, step-by-step help, and custom visual aids. When we compared pre- and post-test scores, the difference was clear. Students using only standard web tools improved their scores by 5.3 percentage points. But students with access to Guided Learning improved by 8.1 percentage points, representing 1.5x higher learning gains in just a single study session. While that number might seem modest — these gains were achieved in just half a day of study, pointing to growing evidence that when technology guides students rather than shortcutting the process, it can lead to more learning. Giving teachers more insight and control Bringing Guided Learning into Google Classroom requires a specialized approach that is purpose-built for the classroom, keeps teachers in control, and grounds the experience in relevant lesson materials. To test this experience, we partnered with Ark and ran a four-week pilot across three UK secondary schools, allowing teachers to use Guided Learning in Google Classroom across four different subjects. Feedback from post-pilot surveys and interviews was encouraging: teachers found Guided Learning handled initial student questions effectively during independent work, so they had more time to offer targeted, one-on-one help. Meanwhile, the majority of surveyed students said they felt comfortable asking Gemini for help when stuck, and over half said it helped them solve problems on their own. We also received important feedback on areas of improvement. Some teachers wanted clearer visibility into how their students were engaging with the course materials so they could better tailor future lessons. Others voiced a desire to keep their students focused on specific assignments during class time and reduce distractions. We took this feedback back to the team and made direct improvements — including adding insights for educators to show how their students interacted with Guided Learning, and improving the ability for teachers to anchor conversations on uploaded curriculum. Shaped by real educator and student feedback in the classroom, today we're rolling out teacher-led Guided Learning globally in Google Classroom. This feature will help teachers assign their students a Guided Learning experience that will coach students step-by-step on their course materials and track student progress with actionable insights. By grounding our tools in learning science, working alongside educators, and conducting research in real classroom settings, we're eager to continue innovating on tools that support active learning and a deeper understanding. body: Designing responsible AI for learning Nov 03, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link We’re bringing Guided Learning capabilities to Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls. Chris Phillips VP & General Manager, Education Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, is introducing Guided Learning to Google Search and Google Classroom to help students think critically through complex problems. These tools provide step-by-step coaching instead of direct answers to support productive study habits. You can find Guided Learning in Google Classroom today, and we are beginning a pilot program for Search in select U.S. schools later this month. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, explains our focus on building responsible AI for students. We are introducing Guided Learning to Google Search and Google Classroom to support active student problem solving. Guided Learning coaches students through complex topics with step-by-step prompts instead of providing direct final answers. School administrators now have full control to enable or disable AI products for their K-12 student accounts. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, explains that we are adding Guided Learning to Google Search and Classroom to help students think through problems instead of just finding quick answers. This tool acts like a personal coach, using questions to guide students through complex topics step by step. We are also giving school administrators full control to decide which AI tools are available to their students, ensuring technology supports classroom learning. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer If you’ve ever watched a student use AI tools to help with their schoolwork, you’ve probably wondered: Are they actually learning, or just finding a shortcut? Questions like this are important, and they guide our work when building products for learning. We believe technology paired with great educators can unlock incredible learning potential, and we’re focused on building technology responsibly to help students thrive. Today, we’re making important updates to our products used in schools, including building Guided Learning capabilities into Google Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls. Developing products built for learning We believe AI products should support “productive struggle” — enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up. That’s the philosophy behind Guided Learning. In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we’re now bringing Guided Learning to more products. Google Search: We’re building Guided Learning capabilities into Search for student accounts to help them work through problems without skipping straight to answers. When our systems understand a student is looking for certain types of homework help, Search will walk them through the topic or problem step by step. For example, if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer. We’re starting with a pilot in select U.S. schools later this month to gather and incorporate educator feedback before expanding to other school districts in the coming months. Google Classroom: Starting today, Guided Learning is globally available in Google Classroom, a central hub where teachers and students organize schoolwork, share assignments and stay connected. When a student starts a Guided Learning activity assigned by their teacher, it acts like a 1-1 study tool, anchored in class material to help them stay on task. It also gives teachers real-time insights to spot where the class might need extra support. Before launching Guided Learning in Google Classroom, we worked closely with schools and educators to test the feature and integrate their feedback. Enhancing school controls We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach. After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on. We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition. Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit. We’ll continue to listen to feedback and evolve our approach as we work in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts, and parents on helping the next generation learn and thrive. title: Expanding AI educator training to new countries
body: Expanding AI educator training to new countries Nov 03, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link The Google AI Educator Series is expanding to five new countries: Spain, Brazil, Mexico, Australia, and sub-Saharan Africa. Here’s how teachers are already using it around the globe. Jennie Magiera Global Head of Education Impact Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We created the Google AI Educator Series to provide teachers with practical skills for using AI. Our training program is currently available in several countries and will soon reach more regions. Educators use these tools to create engaging lessons, save time on tasks, and support student learning. We are launching new November modules to help teachers build assessments and guide game-based learning activities. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Teachers around the world strive to find better ways to overcome challenges and meet each students' unique needs, and many have discovered how AI can become a powerful assistant in this effort. That's why we created the Google AI Educator Series (GES): a no-cost, on-demand training designed to give educators practical AI skills they can use immediately and that fits into their busy schedule. We first launched GES in the U.S earlier this year , and later expanded to India , Korea , Malaysia , Philippines, and the U.K & Ireland. In the coming months, we’re bringing GES to Brazil, Mexico, Spain, Australia, and sub-Saharan Africa. A look at GES from teachers around the world Here is a look at how educators around the world are turning their training into practical applications that save time, make lessons more engaging, and support student learning: India: Teachers are using Gemini and Gemini Notebook to turn complex topics into comic strips, podcasts & infographics – making learning more accessible and engaging. Following September sessions that trained 80,000 educators, we’re bringing GES to all Indian educators with self-paced online modules . Aligned with National Education Policy 2020 , the training is available in English & six local languages — Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Assamese, Odia, Punjabi — with more coming next year. Philippines: Educators are using Gemini to simulate complex market scenarios in economics classes and more, all to free up time for direct student guidance. To support this progress, we’ve partnered with the Philippine Department of Education , Commission on Higher Education , and Technical Skills Development Authority to bring AI training to over one million educators across the country. Building on this momentum, the Philippine Department of Education recently issued an official memorandum endorsing GES to all teaching and non-teaching staff nationwide. Malaysia: Following the official launch of GES at BETT Asia , Malaysian teachers report saving three to five hours of prep time on curricula, assessments, and visual aids per topic, allowing them to focus on interactive, student-centered learning. As a next step, we are launching "train-the-trainer" bootcamps alongside local partners to expand GES training to private school educators , pre-service teachers , and university faculty nationwide. United Kingdom: In the U.K ., teachers are using tools like Gemini Notebook to develop learners’ creative writing skills and create engaging lesson plans and visuals. Through the launch of GES, all 650,000 teachers can receive digital literacy training by joining virtual or in-person events around the UK and Ireland. We are also hosting “ train the trainer ” workshops in the Google London office in November. Korea: In partnership with Seoul National University of Education (SNUE), GES in Korea is aligned with the 2022 Revised Curriculum and the Ministry of Education's Teacher AI/Digital Education Competency Framework. Teachers are using Gemini and Gemini Notebook to design inquiry-based lessons and assessments while streamlining administrative tasks like parent communications and data analysis. New November sessions To ensure GES lessons are truly helpful, we update and create new content monthly in response to feedback from educators. Our November modules go live on November 4th in the U.S. focused on helping educators save time where they tell us they need it most. Here's what's coming: Build interactive assessments: Learn how to use Gemini to build practice tests and interactive web assessments — like exit tickets with instant feedback and hints for incorrect answers — to help students prepare for assessments like state exams.. Guide students through game-based learning: Guide students through interactive, game-based learning experiences that demonstrate the importance of data accuracy, model performance, and human oversight. Strengthen academic assignments: Use Gemini to learn how to spot questions that can lead to taking shortcuts, helping faculty strengthen assignments and encourage deeper student critical thinking. Generative AI is experimental. We are scaling our defenses across Asia Pacific to protect people from complex, organized scam networks. We are strengthening our defenses against complex scams across the Asia Pacific region. Our new Android features now detect AI-driven impersonation calls and alert you to suspicious messages. We are also working with industry partners to share threat intelligence and providing 6 million dollars in funding to local organizations. These efforts help you, small businesses, and communities recognize fraud, stay safe online, and build resilience against organized crime groups. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Scams are growing more complex, fueled by increasingly sophisticated tactics from transnational crime groups. A recent UN report illustrated the effect these scams have across the Asia Pacific (APAC) region. In 2025, scam losses across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand reached up to $114.1 billion USD, with over 40% of ASEAN consumers said to be experiencing scams. Tackling these highly organized networks requires a unified effort. Today, we are sharing how, at Google, we are scaling our defenses to protect APAC communities. This includes built-in protections across products and platforms, industry-wide collaboration, and new local partnerships to increase community resilience. Built-in protections across devices and platforms Our first line of defense is to secure the devices and platforms people use every day. This year, Android launched Fake Call Detection , a feature designed to spot AI-driven phone call impersonation. Built on open RCS technology, other platforms can adopt the same protections. On Pixel, built-in scam detection now alerts you to potential scams from many popular messaging apps. We are partnering to bring this to additional Android users later this year . We are also expanding Android developer verification to protect people against malicious apps outside Google Play, wherever apps are distributed. Industry alignment for collective defense Beyond product solutions, defeating fraud networks requires coordination across experts and industries. Earlier this year, we joined industry peers to sign the Industry Accord Against Online Scams and Fraud , taking a collective approach to sharing threat intelligence and coordinating defenses. Building on the Industry Accord, we recently helped establish the Japan Anti-Scam Alliance (JASA) to enable public and private institutions to deploy aligned defenses. Google.org also recently helped launch the Global Anti-Scams Philanthropy Collaborative to coordinate cross-industry philanthropic action against scams globally. Efforts to strengthen community resilience To strengthen resilience at the community level, today Google.org announced $6 million in funding to The Asia Foundation and the Tech for Good Institute to help small businesses and individuals in APAC to stay safe online. The efforts will include training local communities on building scam resilience, incubating AI-powered defense prototypes, and equipping policymakers with insights to strengthen threat measures. This builds on Google.org’s ongoing support for local organizations, like Bamboo Builders in Singapore and the Taiwan FactCheck Center, to deliver specialized, hyper-local training to citizens. And it expands on the ASEAN Foundation’s Scam Ready ASEAN initiative, which is bringing online scam prevention resources to millions in the region. We are also expanding Be Scam Ready , an educational scam-awareness game — and one of the Scam Ready ASEAN’s program resources — to Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. Be Scam Ready simulates common scams to prepare citizens, and is already available in Singapore, Thailand, and Taiwan. Helping communities stay ahead of organized fraud is central to our work, and we will continue to advocate for a collaborative, global approach. title: Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia
body: Press Release Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia WASHINGTON – Abraham Teklu Lemma, 54, a former information technology contractor at the U.S. Department of State, the U.S. Department of Justice, and the National Reconnaissance Office, pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. “For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.” Senior Judge John D. Bates scheduled sentencing for April 14, 2027. “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” “Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.” According to court papers, Lemma, of Silver Spring, Maryland, held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance who, from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States. Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government. During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings. Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities.  Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked. On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].” According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §794.  If accepted by the Court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office. The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division. 24cr573 Follow us on X , Instagram , and YouTube Or at https://www.justice.gov/usao-dc Updated November 3, 2026 Topic National Security Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - District of Columbia

title: Oklahoma Man Charged in Connection with Sending Threatening Letters Containing Non-Toxic White Powder to Election and Government Officials Across the Country
body: Press Release Oklahoma Man Charged in Connection with Sending Threatening Letters Containing Non-Toxic White Powder to Election and Government Officials Across the Country Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Robin Patrick Martin, 67, of Oklahoma City, has been charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in connection with threatening letters mailed to state election officials, members of Congress, the FBI and others. “As alleged, Martin mailed letters containing white powder to hundreds of state and federal officials, a calculated attempt to terrorize public servants,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These officials were left to open those letters not knowing if the powder inside could sicken or even kill them, and that was the evident intent. Intimidation like this has no place in a Nation governed by the rule of law, and the National Security Division will investigate and prosecute these cases to the fullest extent appropriate.” “Threatening election officials and attempting to intimidate public servants is a serious federal offense and will not be tolerated,” said U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester for the Western District of Oklahoma. “Working alongside our federal law enforcement partners, we are committed to investigating these threats and holding accountable those who seek to spread fear and intimidation in our communities.” “Early Monday morning, the FBI conducted an operation and arrested Robin Patrick Martin – the subject who allegedly sent hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder substances to public officials around the country both before the 2024 and 2026 election,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The letters went to well over 100 locations including multiple state secretary offices, election offices, and more. The alleged subject had avoided authorities until now – as the Biden administration failed to catch him – but this FBI got it done. I want to thank our Oklahoma City Field Office and the FBI Criminal Division, as well as our USPIS, Capitol Police, and OKC PD partners who responded to the threat quickly and did outstanding work executing in this case. Every American citizen deserves a free and fair election – and anyone who attempts to undermine that process by breaking our laws and threatening public officials will be brought to justice.” “The mailing of letters containing an unknown powdery substance across the country created unnecessary fear, diverted resources, and attempted to disrupt our nation’s democratic process,” said Special Agent in Charge Doug Goodwater of the FBI Oklahoma City Field Office. “No one should have to wonder whether a letter in the mail poses a danger, and the arrest of Robin Martin demonstrates that those who seek to spread panic and intimidation cannot expect to remain anonymous. I would like to express my gratitude to the dedicated team at FBI Oklahoma City and our partners at the US Attorney’s Offices, USPIS, USPS, U.S. Capitol Police, FBI Laboratory Division, and Oklahoma City Department for all their work in this matter.” “The Postal Inspection Service has a long, proud, and successful history of ensuring the sanctity of election mail, safeguarding the integrity of elections, and protecting election officials from threatening and dangerous mail,” said Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS). “Utilizing our expertise in the Postal Service and mail flow, postal inspectors and our partners identified related mailings and recovered the majority of these mailings before they reached their intended recipients, keeping Postal Service customers — the American public — safe. This arrest reflects the perseverance of the Postal Inspection Service, FBI, U.S. Capitol Police, and all of our law enforcement partners to keep criminals from interfering with two trusted traditions — the election process, and the U.S. Mail.” “Our team has been working around the clock with our law enforcement partners to put this defendant behind bars,” said U.S. Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan. “We will not tolerate anyone who attempts to use fear as a weapon.” According to public records, on Oct. 13, 2026, the Oklahoma State Election Board notified the FBI that it had received a threatening letter containing white powder. The FBI and USPIS had been investigating threatening letters containing white powder sent to multiple state election officials — including the Oklahoma State Election Board — since 2024. The FBI and USPIS determined that this letter was part of hundreds of threatening letters, many of which had white powder, that had been sent across the country to state election boards, members of Congress, election pollsters, media organizations, and others. The white powder was later determined to be non-hazardous. Today, Martin appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin for his initial appearance in Oklahoma City. This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House-directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence. This case is being investigated by the FBI, USPIS, United States Capitol Police, Oklahoma City Police Department, and Texas Department of Public Safety, including the Texas Rangers, with valuable assistance from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Oklahoma. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Oklahoma is prosecuting the case with assistance from the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section. A complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Note : Read the complaint here . Updated November 3, 2026 Topic National Security Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) National Security Division (NSD) USAO - Oklahoma, Western Press Release Number: 26-1315
retained_feed_body: Robin Patrick Martin, 67, of Oklahoma City, has been charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in connection with threatening letters mailed to state election officials, members of Congress, the FBI and others.

title: Man Pleads Guilty to Sexually Exploiting a Child in Vinton, Iowa, and to Possessing Child Pornography
body: Press Release Man Pleads Guilty to Sexually Exploiting a Child in Vinton, Iowa, and to Possessing Child Pornography Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Iowa A man who sexually exploited a child in Vinton, Iowa, in 2022, pled guilty today in federal court in Cedar Rapids.  Dennis Tomas Greehy, age 38, most recently from Melbourne, Florida, was convicted of sexual exploitation of a child and possession of child pornography. In a plea agreement, Greehy admitted that he started talking online with a 13‑year‑old child in 2020.  He asked the child to send him nude photos and videos, and the child did so.  On multiple occasions, starting when the child was 14 years old, Greehy traveled from North Carolina to Iowa City and had sex with the child.  In the summer of 2022, he rented an apartment in Vinton and he had sex with the child in that apartment.  He also recorded the child engaging in sexually explicit conduct.  Greehy then moved to Florida but continued to communicate with the child, asking for photos and videos of the child engaged in sex acts.  He also traveled back to Iowa to have sex with the child.  In June 2026, law enforcement officers arrested Greehy in Florida and seized his phone.  On his phone were several depictions of the child engaging in sexually explicit conduct. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice.  Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims.  For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC . Sentencing before United States District Court Chief Judge C.J. Williams will be set after a presentence report is prepared.  Greehy remains in custody of the United States Marshal pending sentencing.  Greehy faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years’ imprisonment and a possible maximum sentence of 40 years’ imprisonment, a $500,000 fine, $77,200 in special assessments, and a lifetime term of supervised release following any imprisonment. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Devra T. Hake and was investigated by the Iowa City Police Department, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Brevard County, Florida, Sheriff’s Office, and the Melbourne, Florida, Police Department. Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl . The case file number is 26-CR-46. Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA. title: Maryland Man Pleads Guilty to Role in Tax and COVID-Fraud Conspiracy
body: Press Release Maryland Man Pleads Guilty to Role in Tax and COVID-Fraud Conspiracy Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maryland Baltimore, Maryland – A Maryland man pled guilty in federal court to tax and COVID-related fraud charges. This prosecution is part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. Dekwii Woah-Tee, 43, of Rosedale, pled guilty to conspiracy to submit false, fictitious, and fraudulent claims to the Internal Revenue Service; wire-fraud conspiracy in connection with Unemployment Insurance (UI) claims for benefits; and aggravated identity theft stemming from a scheme to fraudulently obtain UI benefits during the COVID-19 Pandemic. Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the guilty plea with Executive Special Agent in Charge Kareem Carter, Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Washington D.C. Field Office; Inspector General Anthony P. D’Esposito, U.S. Department of Labor - Office of Inspector General (DOL-OIG); and Joseph V. Cuffari Ph.D., Inspector General, Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS-OIG). According to the plea agreement, beginning in January 2018, and continuing until December 2024, Dekwii Woah-Tee and his co-conspirators conspired to defraud the United States and the Department of the Treasury by filing fraudulent Form 1040s seeking tax refunds from the IRS through false claims.  The co-conspirators identified and recruited individuals to become customers of their tax-return business and obtained tax documentation and personal identifiable information from those individuals seeking tax-return preparation assistance. Dekwii Woah-Tee and his co-conspirators used the information obtained from those individuals to prepare tax filings with the IRS. Then he and his co-conspirators filed or caused the filing of false tax returns, which contained fabricated information regarding the taxpayer’s dependents, income, education expenses, and eligibility for the Earned Income Tax Credit. The co-conspirators caused the IRS to deposit funds into bank accounts or to deliver treasury checks to addresses that they controlled. As a result, the co-conspirators obtained tax refunds they were not entitled to in connection with submitting tax returns in which they illegally sought at least $3.5 million in refunds. Dekwii Woah-Tee pleaded guilty to wire fraud, wire fraud conspiracy, and aggravated identity theft arising out of his scheme to unlawfully obtain UI benefits during the COVID-19 Pandemic.  Dekwii Woah-Tee and his co-conspirator Daiwor Woah-Tee, who pled guilty to charges connected to his role in the conspiracy in June 2026, submitted UI applications to the Maryland Department of Labor on behalf of victims, often without the victim’s knowledge, falsely stating that the applicant was entitled to UI benefits.  As a result, the co-conspirators caused the Maryland Department of Labor to deposit UI benefits into bank accounts that they controlled, allowing them to withdraw the funds for their own personal use.  The co-conspirators received UI benefits in excess of $550,000. As part of the plea, Dekwii Woah-Tee agreed to restitution to the Internal Revenue Service of $3.5 million and restitution to the Maryland Department of Labor of at least $550,000.  Dekwii Woah-Tee also agreed to a forfeiture of approximately $250,000. If convicted, Dekwii Woah-Tee faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison for conspiracy to submit false, fictitious, and fraudulent claims to the Internal Revenue Service. He is also facing 20 years for wire-fraud conspiracy in connection with Unemployment Insurance claims for benefits and a mandatory two years for aggravated identity theft. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The District of Maryland Strike Force is one of five strike forces established throughout the United States by the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate and prosecute COVID-19 fraud, including fraud relating to the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (“CARES”) Act.  The CARES Act was designed to provide emergency financial assistance to Americans suffering the economic effects caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.  The strike forces focus on large-scale, multi-state pandemic relief fraud perpetrated by criminal organizations and transnational actors.  The strike forces are interagency law enforcement efforts, using prosecutor-led and data analyst-driven teams designed to identify and bring to justice those who stole pandemic relief funds. For more information on the Department’s response to the pandemic, please visit justice.gov/coronavirus .  Anyone with information about allegations of attempted fraud involving COVID-19 can report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at 866-720-5721 or via the NCDF Web Complaint Form at: justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form . U.S. Attorney Hayes commended the IRS-CI, DOL-OIG, and DHS-OIG for their work in the investigation.  Ms. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jared W. Murphy and Matthew P. Phelps who are prosecuting this federal case. For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to report fraud, visit justice.gov/usao-md and justice.gov/usao-md/report-fraud . # # # Contact Kevin Nash USAMD.Press@usdoj.gov 410-209-4946 Updated November 3, 2026 Topics Benefit Fraud COVID-Related Fraud Identity Theft Tax Components National Fraud Enforcement Division USAO - Maryland

title: Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia
body: Press Release Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” “For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.” “Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.” “Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.” According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States. Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government. During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings. Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked. On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].” According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027. The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office. The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division. Updated November 3, 2026 Topic National Security Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) National Security Division (NSD) USAO - District of Columbia Press Release Number: 26-1314

title: Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Results in Record Powder Fentanyl Seizure and Federal Charges
body: Press Release Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Results in Record Powder Fentanyl Seizure and Federal Charges Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Mexico Prosecution is part of Homeland Security Task Force effort to combat transnational criminal organizations Statement from U.S. Attorney’s Office and DEA El Paso Division ALBUQUERQUE – An Albuquerque woman is facing federal drug trafficking and firearm offenses after an HSTF investigation allegedly recovered large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, cash, and firearms from her Albuquerque residence. According to court documents, law enforcement is investigating a drug trafficking organization allegedly importing large quantities of fentanyl, heroin and other narcotics into Albuquerque, New Mexico. On October 28, 2026, a U.S. Magistrate Judge authorized a federal search warrant for the residence of Angel Ramirez , 45, in northwest Albuquerque. On October 29, 2026, agents executed the warrant and encountered Ramirez , the sole adult in the home. Inside the master bedroom, investigators allegedly located multiple duffel bags containing large quantities of narcotics, bulk U.S. currency, and numerous firearms. Laboratory field testing confirmed the presence of fentanyl and heroin. Bulk quantities of cash and fentanyl and other narcotics seized from Ramirez’s house Numerous firearms seized from Ramirez’s house In total, agents recovered approximately 43.75 kilograms of fentanyl powder, the largest seizure in New Mexico in the DEA history, 7.70 kilograms of fentanyl pills, 4.40 kilograms of heroin, and an additional 1,036 grams of fentanyl in a separate container. Investigators also located approximately 29 firearms and assorted ammunition inside and around a gun safe directly beneath the narcotics and cash. Court documents state that Ramirez was employed as a paralegal with the State of New Mexico’s Department of Justice, a taxpayer‑funded position of public trust. Investigators allege that Ramirez leveraged her government employment, clean criminal history, and internal access to the justice system to create a veneer of legitimacy while her residence operated as a distribution hub for narcotics, drug proceeds, and firearms. “Nearly 50 kilograms of fentanyl powder in a single Albuquerque home tells us just how serious the drug trafficking problem has become in New Mexico,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “This is a tremendous accomplishment by the agents who got these drugs off our streets, but it is no cause for celebration. With fentanyl overdose deaths on the rise in New Mexico, we have a lot more work to do. We will continue targeting the organizations bringing these drugs into our state and aggressively prosecuting those responsible.” “As members of the community, I want you to know that our agents remain deeply committed to protecting and serving the city of Albuquerque,” said DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda. “I’m proud of their professionalism, dedication, and the outstanding work they demonstrated throughout this operation.  DEA remains steadfast in our mission to keep our communities safe.” Ramirez is charged with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime. She will remain in custody pending trial which has not been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Ramirez faces no less than 15 years and up to life in prison. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison made the announcement today on behalf of HSTF.  Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Probasco, Timothy Piatt and Oliver Stephanz are prosecuting the case. This arrest is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Region II CORE 7 is comprised of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Customs and Border Protection – Office of Field Operations (OFO), U.S. Border Patrol (USBP) and Air and Marine (AMO), Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), United States Department of the Interior – Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Joint Task Force North (JTF-N), United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), United States Marshal Service (USMS), Department of State, Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DSS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Texas Department of Public Safety (TXDPS), El Paso Police Department (EPPD), New Mexico State Police (NMSP), West Texas / New Mexico High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA), Albuquerque Police Department, New Mexico Sixth Judicial District, Las Cruces/Dona Ana County Metro Narcotics Agency, and the prosecution is being led by the Office of the United States Attorney for the Districts of Western Texas and New Mexico. The Sandoval County Sheriff’s Office, Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office, Rio Rancho Police Department and Pueblo of Pojoaque Tribal Police Department provided invaluable assistance in this arrest. A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ramirez_complaint.pdf ramirez_motion_to_detain.pdf Updated November 3, 2026 Topic Homeland Security Task Force Components Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - New Mexico Press Release Number: 26-298

title: Illegal Alien from the Dominican Republic Charged with Healthcare Benefit Fraud and Aggravated Identity Theft
body: Press Release Illegal Alien from the Dominican Republic Charged with Healthcare Benefit Fraud and Aggravated Identity Theft Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts Defendant allegedly convicted of multiple felonies under stolen identity of U.S. citizen. BOSTON – A Dominican man unlawfully residing in Salem, Mass. was charged by criminal complaint allegedly unlawfully obtaining approximately $16,000 in MassHealth benefits and aggravated identity theft. Cledis German Romero, 40, has been charged with healthcare benefit fraud and aggravated identity theft and appeared in federal court in Boston on Nov. 3, 2026. He has been detained pending further proceedings. According to the charging documents, German Romero allegedly used the stolen identity of a U.S. citizen to obtain Massachusetts state driver’s licenses and healthcare benefits, including approximately $16,205 in MassHealth benefits. German Romero also allegedly used the stolen identity of the U.S. citizen in connection with multiple arrests and criminal convictions in Massachusetts, including resisting arrest and conspiracy to violate the controlled substances act. The charge of making false statements relating to a health care program provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The charge of aggravated identity theft provides for a mandatory consecutive sentence of two years and one year of supervised release. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. On March 26, 2026 , United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced the creation of the Benefit & Voter Fraud Team, a district-wide initiative established in response to the rampant fraud being uncovered across Massachusetts. Members of the public are encouraged to report suspected benefit fraud in Massachusetts by calling 1-855-SCAM-MA-1 (855-722-6621). On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law. title: Strand Book Store, Inc. to Pay Nearly $1.5 Million for Improper Receipt of Paycheck Protection Program Loan
body: Press Release Strand Book Store, Inc. to Pay Nearly $1.5 Million for Improper Receipt of Paycheck Protection Program Loan Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia WASHINGTON – The United States Attorney for the District of Columbia announced today that Strand Book Store, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,482,560 because the New York City bookstore violated the False Claims Act by improperly applying for and receiving a second draw loan under the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) for which it was not eligible. Strand was ineligible because Senator Ron Wyden’s wife was the owner. “The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Strand Book Store, owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, received $932,350 in second draw PPP funds despite a federal law barring businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving those loans. Our Fraud and Asset Recovery Division will expose this abuse, pursue those who exploit taxpayer dollars, and hold them accountable. No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.” When Congress enacted the Coronavirus, Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act in March 2020, it authorized forgivable PPP loans to eligible small businesses and nonprofit organizations for job retention and certain other expenses. The PPP loan program was administered by the Small Business Administration. In the Economic Aid to Hard-Hit Small Businesses, Nonprofits, and Venues Act enacted in December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for PPP loans and allowed eligible entities to apply for a “second draw” of PPP funding. The Economic Aid Act included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant. In February 2021, Strand applied for a second draw PPP loan in the amount of $932,350. At the time, the controlling owner of Strand was Nancy Bass Wyden, the wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden. On behalf of Strand, Ms. Wyden made a number of certifications as part of the loan application, including that the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant. Ms. Wyden’s certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received. The settlement resolves claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act. Under these provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of the recovery. The qui tam complaint was filed by a corporate Relator Blockquote Inc. and is captioned U.S. ex rel. Blockquote Inc. v. Strand Book Store, Inc., Civ. No. 25-3609 (D.D.C.) . Blockquote Inc. will receive a total share of approximately $148,256 in connection with the settlement. The civil settlement resulted from an investigation by Assistant United States Attorney Sean M. Tepe with the support of attorney Christopher J. McClintock of SBA’s Office of the General Counsel. This is the second recovery on behalf of the United States since U.S. Attorney Pirro announced the creation of the Fraud and Asset Recovery Division, headed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Dan Schiffer. Tips and complaint regarding potential fraud affecting COVID-19 government relief programs can be reported by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at (866) 720-5721 or by submitting a NCDF Web Complaint form at https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form . On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The claims resolved by the civil settlement are allegations only, and there has been no determination of liability. ## 25cv3609 Follow us on X , Instagram , and YouTube or at https://www.justice.gov/usao-dc Updated November 3, 2026 Topics Benefit Fraud COVID-Related Fraud Component USAO - District of Columbia

title: Illegal Alien from Dominican Republic Indicted for Unlawful Reentry
body: Press Release Illegal Alien from Dominican Republic Indicted for Unlawful Reentry Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts Defendant previously convicted of unlawful reentry. BOSTON – A Dominican man unlawfully residing in Lynn was indicted by a federal grand jury for unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation. Cesar Fernando Guerrero-Casado, 41, was indicted for illegally reentering the United States after deportation. The defendant is currently detained in state custody on unrelated charges and appeared in federal court on Nov. 2, 2026. According to the indictment, Guerrero-Casado was previously removed from the United States on Feb. 24, 2015. It is alleged that sometime after his February 2015 removal, Guerrero-Casado illegally reentered the United States without permission. Guerrero-Casado was previously convicted of unlawful reentry in 2014. He is currently serving state prison sentences for drug offenses. The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law. Updated November 3, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: Palmetto Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Disposal of a Deceased Body
body: Press Release Palmetto Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Disposal of a Deceased Body Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Florida Tampa, Florida – Matthew Edward Zoladz (37, Palmetto) has pleaded guilty to one count of violating the Marine Protection, Research, and Sanctuaries Act, and one count of violating the Act to Prevent Pollution from Ships. He faces a maximum penalty of 15 years in federal prison. Zoladz will be sentenced on January 20, 2027. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement. According to court documents, on or about December 7, 2022, Zoladz and Victim 1 engaged in drug use together, during which time Victim 1 overdosed and passed away. Zoladz drove around with Victim 1’s unconscious or deceased body in the front seat of his vehicle and took a video of Victim 1. On or about December 8, 2022, Zoladz was scheduled to work as a deckhand on a vessel. Prior to the departure of the vessel, Zoladz wrapped Victim 1’s body in a plastic trash bag and loaded Victim 1’s body onto the ship. That evening, while the ship was out at sea, Zoladz dumped the plastic trash bag containing Victim 1’s body into ocean waters. This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Abigail K. King and E. Jackson Boggs, Jr. Updated November 3, 2026 Component USAO - Florida, Middle

Zoladz will be sentenced on January 20, 2027. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

title: St. Louis Man Charged with Firearms Offense
body: Press Release St. Louis Man Charged with Firearms Offense Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Missouri JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A St. Louis, Mo., man appeared in federal court today before Chief U.S. Magistrate Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr. on a complaint alleging that he possessed a firearm after a prior felony conviction. According to the affidavit filed in support of the complaint, Iseah Christopher Jackson, 23, was identified by law enforcement as having been present during a shooting in the area of Ninth Street and Walnut Street in Columbia on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. Later that day, a traffic stop was conducted on his vehicle and a loaded 9mm semi-automatic handgun was found in his glove compartment. Jackson also had a single round of 9mm ammunition in his pocket at the time of his arrest. The affidavit notes that Jackson was previously convicted of two counts of involuntary manslaughter arising out of his involvement in a shooting resulting in the death of two individuals. Due to these prior felony convictions, Jackson is not permitted to possess a firearm. The charges contained in the complaint are accusations, and not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must eventually be presented to a federal trial jury, whose duty it is to determine guilt or innocence. This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren E. Kummerer. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. Project Safe Neighborhoods Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Updated November 3, 2026 Topic Project Safe Neighborhoods Component USAO - Missouri, Western

title: Seffner Man Sentenced to 24 years, Consecutive to 25-year State Prison Sentence, for Production and Distribution of Child Sexual Abuse Material
body: Press Release Seffner Man Sentenced to 24 years, Consecutive to 25-year State Prison Sentence, for Production and Distribution of Child Sexual Abuse Material Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Florida Tampa, FL – Joel Reynolds (48, Seffner) has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Thomas P. Barber to 24 years in federal prison for production, distribution, and possession of child sexual abuse material. The court ordered the sentence to run consecutive to Reynolds’s 25-year state prison sentence. Reynolds pleaded to the federal offenses on July 9, 2026. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement. According to court documents, law enforcement initiated an investigation into Reynolds after receiving a cyber tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children in November 2024. Further investigation revealed    Reynolds had produced child sexual abuse material and distributed at least one such image on a social media application. Law enforcement discovered Reynolds in possession of hundreds of videos depicting minors engaged in sexually explicit conduct on his devices. This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Courtney Derry. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. title: Fort Myers Man Sentenced to More than 21 Years in Federal Prison for Child Exploitation Offenses
body: Press Release Fort Myers Man Sentenced to More than 21 Years in Federal Prison for Child Exploitation Offenses Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Florida Fort Myers, Florida – Rudy Perez (41, Fort Myers) has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Sheri Polster Chappell to 21 years and 8 months in federal prison for enticing minors to engage in sexual activity, receiving and possessing images and videos depicting the sexual abuse of children, and transferring obscene matter to a minor. Perez was found guilty on August 3, 2026, following a bench trial. Perez was also sentenced to a term of life of supervised release and ordered to register as a sex offender. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement. According to court documents, between January and April 2022, Perez used a social media application to persuade, induce, and entice a minor to engage in sexual activity. In January 2025, a social media application made a Cybertipline Report to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) that Perez was involved with the online enticement of children for sexual acts. During the course of the investigation, law enforcement obtained a search warrant for Perez’s social media account. The FBI observed that Perez had enticed and solicited numerous other users who had identified themselves as children for sexually explicit images, and several minor children sent sexually explicit material to Perez at his request. Further, Perez sent photographs and sexually explicit videos and images of adults to numerous users who had identified themselves as children. Pursuant to a search warrant, Perez’s cellphone was seized and a subsequent forensic analysis revealed that Perez possessed child sexual abuse material, including numerous videos depicting the sexual abuse of minors. This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Fort Myers Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, which includes the Lee County Sheriff’s Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Yolande G. Viacava. This is another case brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc. Updated November 3, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Florida, Middle
