title: Google Messages, Phone by Google, and Google Contacts get new, updated icons.
body: Google Messages, Phone by Google, and Google Contacts get new, updated icons. Nov 02, 2026 Starting today, we’re rolling out refreshed icons for three apps that help you stay connected: Google Messages, Phone by Google, and Google Contacts. These are the same apps you trust and use every day, now with enhanced icons designed with your feedback in mind. The new icons are sharper and clearer on your home screen. For example, we’ve added a subtle but crisp gradient with easily readable edges. They also feature updated curvature and coloring to align with the rest of the Google apps you know and love, such as our core Google logo . Don’t worry, the functionality of these apps isn’t changing as a result of the new icons. You’ll simply spot a sleeker, more cohesive look on your home screen in the coming weeks. Check out the conversation on our community forum for more.

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)
body: AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026) The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions , which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it. The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock , and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex. AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate , which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate , which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher. AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs. Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2 , and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR , point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks : lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x. Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager . Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service , producing the evidence its regulator needed. How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog. Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. title: Boris Vujčić: Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world
body:
Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Boris Vujčić Vice-President of the European Central Bank SPEECH Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world Speech by Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB, at the Central Bank of Ireland’s Financial System Conference Dublin, 2 November 2026 Thank you to the Central Bank of Ireland for organising this conference and inviting me to speak. It is a great pleasure to be here in Dublin. Ireland illustrates why the topics of today’s event – from geopolitics to financial resilience – are timely. Ireland has one of the most open economies in the world and it is deeply integrated into European and global markets. It is a Single Market success story, and a reminder that openness remains one of Europe’s greatest strengths. But openness works both ways. A shift in US trade policy or a turn in global capital flows can spill over to the Irish economy particularly quickly. What is true for Ireland is also true on a larger scale for the EU, the world’s largest trading bloc. [ 1 ] So, the question I would like to discuss today is simple to ask but harder to answer: how do we retain the benefits of an open economy in a more uncertain world increasingly shaped by geopolitics? My answer in a single sentence is: not by retreating from openness, but by building the resilience that allows this openness to endure. Geopolitics is becoming economics Let me start with the environment we are facing. Geopolitical shocks are becoming more frequent. They affect growth and inflation directly, and they can threaten financial stability. We have seen this repeatedly in recent years. Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have triggered severe disruptions in energy markets. Tariffs have renewed uncertainty and redirected global trade flows, while restrictions on exports of critical technologies and raw materials have reinforced the value of strategic autonomy (Slide 2, left-hand side). Alongside these developments, we have seen sanctions regimes, cyber threats and a step change in security and defence spending. The result is a different macroeconomic environment. Inflation, for example, is now driven more often by supply shocks – in the past six years supply factors have played a role in three major shocks: in 2020, 2022 and 2026. And we are faced with more volatile energy prices as well as greater uncertainty about the outlook (Slide 2, right-hand side). These shocks can also be transmitted through financial channels. Bond and equity prices may come under pressure, while investment funds could face outflows that amplify market movements. [ 2 ] Banks exposed to affected countries, sectors or markets may experience losses that weigh on capital or raise funding costs, potentially leading them to tighten lending. [ 3 ] So far, the financial system has absorbed each of these shocks remarkably well. But financial effects can be highly non-linear and typically emerge abruptly: past resilience is no reason for complacency. Common in origin, uneven in impact We cannot prevent geopolitical shocks. And pulling back from the world would not shield us from such shocks: while a fragmenting world means fewer links, it also means that those links are more concentrated. The result is less diversification and higher risk. Energy is the clearest, and unfortunately a recurring, example. The EU imports 57% of its energy, and almost all of its oil and gas. Before 2022, much of that came from Russia. That is why Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused the EU’s largest energy shock since the 1970s. Europe responded. We diversified our energy supplies by increasing liquefied natural gas (LNG) import capacity and reduced our dependence on Russia. This is an important achievement. But diversification alone could not shield us when tensions erupted in the Middle East earlier this year. This showed us that exposure is only half the story.  The other half is about resilience – in other words, how well we absorb the shocks. For the financial sector, resilience means strong capital and liquidity buffers, diversified funding, and payment and settlement systems that can withstand operational and cyber threats. But there is also a broader, economy-wide dimension to resilience – one that is becoming increasingly important for Europe. In a more competitive and uncertain global environment, resilience requires stronger mechanisms for sharing risks and diversifying supply chains across countries and markets. Coming back to the example of the energy shocks, they hit every Member State differently. How hard they land depends on a country’s energy mix, its trade links and the structure of its financial system. Take 2022: electricity prices for firms rose far more, and stayed high far longer, in Italy than in Spain – and part of the difference is that Spain generates much more of its power from renewables (Slide 3). Two encouraging points follow from this. First, our energy supply is already more resilient than in 2022. As the energy mix shifts towards low-carbon sources, wholesale electricity prices have become less sensitive to gas prices, including since the start of the war in the Middle East. [ 4 ] Second, shocks that are common in origin but uneven in impact have already shown how European risk sharing can cushion country-specific effects and strengthen resilience across the EU. This shows that the lessons about how Europe can enhance its resilience are not the same as those for other large economies such as the United States and China, which automatically benefit from scale. Europe needs to find its strength in the depth of its integration – rising above the Member State perspective towards a truly European perspective. Europe’s untapped strength: a truly single market Today, fragmentation prevents us from realising our European potential. Too often, national rules, standards and procedures diverge, forcing companies to navigate multiple legal and regulatory regimes when they operate across borders. These differences act like internal tariffs: according to ECB estimates, they are equivalent to a tariff of around 67% for goods and 95% for services. [ 5 ] While this is the upper bound of estimates, the message is clear: doing business across borders within the Single Market is expensive. One consequence is a persistent home bias, with capital staying within national borders, alongside a growing allocation of European savings to markets outside the EU. Consider equity markets. Since 2014, estimated tariff-equivalent frictions affecting cross-border equity holdings within the euro area have fallen by around 12 percentage points. Between the euro area and the United States, the decline has been around 25 percentage points, roughly twice as much (Slide 4, left-hand side). [ 6 ] Strikingly, we are integrating faster with the United States than with each other. [ 7 ] As a result, European savings increasingly fund US companies. There are, of course, good reasons to diversify. But in a fragmenting world, this also means greater dependence on a single external partner and leaves our own markets underdeveloped. Venture capital tells a similar story: US funds invest around six times as much as EU-based funds (Slide 4, right-hand side). [ 8 ] Foreign venture capital funds partly fill the gap, but this makes it more likely that successful European start-ups move their headquarters or intellectual property abroad, or choose to list outside the EU. Beyond missing out on growth, a lack of integration weakens risk sharing and therefore resilience. Let me explain why. When a shock hits one country harder than others, integrated systems help share the burden. This holds true for energy and electricity markets, where physical interconnections and common trading hubs foster price convergence. [ 9 ] It is also true for financial markets, where investors operate across borders and regions. Cross-border investors spread gains and losses. Banks operating across borders can help sustain lending where domestic conditions are weak. The numbers are stark. ECB research finds that around 70% of state-level output shocks in the United States are absorbed through markets and fiscal transfers, with capital markets doing most of the work. In the euro area, the overall share is far lower, at around 30%, and capital markets absorb only 5 to 10%. [ 10 ] Two results show what that gap means in practice. European firms cut investment in response to higher oil prices. For US firms, we see no such reduction (Slide 5, left-hand side). [ 11 ] And among European firms most exposed to the COVID-19 shock, those with mostly domestic shareholders cut investment 20% more than their peers with an international shareholder base (Slide 5, right-hand side). [ 12 ] In a fragmented Europe, investment becomes the margin of adjustment whenever a shock hits. That is a resilience problem before it is a growth problem. Integration: our best response and the lever we control We cannot set the trade policy of others. But the openness across borders within our Single Market is entirely within our control. Our broader aim should be to reduce barriers to trade in goods and services and complete the Single Market. And the numbers are on our side. Reducing internal barriers to goods and services by just 2% could, in the long run, offset the projected impact of higher US tariffs on euro area GDP, estimated at around 0.7 percentage points between 2025 and 2027 (Slide 6). [ 13 ] This shows that integration can strengthen resilience and enhance competitiveness at the same time. And again, in light of the two consecutive energy shocks we have faced, energy provides a particularly relevant example. A more interconnected and genuinely integrated energy market, built primarily on renewables, would reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and limit their impact on electricity prices. From a central banking perspective, one of the most important building blocks of the Single Market is the savings and investments union, which targets the financial sector. I am particularly pleased that Commissioner Albuquerque is with us today, as this is a key priority on her agenda and one on which we are closely aligned. I look forward to hearing her reflections on how we can move it forward. Importantly, the savings and investments union encompasses both the banking union and the capital markets union. Cross-border banking groups should be able to operate across the euro area as though it were a single jurisdiction, with capital and liquidity moving freely within the group. That requires completing the missing pillar of the banking union – a European deposit insurance scheme – complemented by a sound crisis management framework. Deposit protection should be equally robust across the euro area, and bank failures should be managed consistently throughout the banking union, supported by more harmonised creditor hierarchies and insolvency rules. We also need a truly integrated European capital market that mobilises savings for productive investment and allows capital to flow freely across the EU. Harmonising withholding taxes is an important part of that effort. And finally, the Single Market cannot function without resilient payment systems. This is why Europe needs its own resilient payments infrastructure: one that keeps working under stress and is European. The digital euro is part of the answer, reducing reliance on non-European retail payment providers. Another part is a European infrastructure for wholesale digital payments. In this regard, the launch of Pontes in September marked an important milestone. Each of these initiatives lowers barriers and makes Europe more integrated and resilient. Together, they help ensure that Europe stays open to the world. Conclusion Let me conclude. The geopolitical environment is unlikely to become any easier. But how well we absorb the shocks we face depends very much on the choices we make. Openness, integration and resilience are not competing goals. They reinforce one another. Integration makes us more resilient. Resilience allows us to remain open. And openness, as Ireland’s experience shows, is one of Europe’s greatest sources of prosperity. Thank you for your attention. Trade openness, measured as the sum of gross exports and imports over output, is significantly higher in the euro area than in the United States. title: Report on U.S. Portfolio Holdings of Foreign Securities at Year-End 2025
body: October 30, 2026 Washington – Fial data from an annual survey of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 were released today and posted on the Treasury web site at https://home.treasury.gov/data/treasury-international-capital-tic-system/tic-forms-instructions/us-claims-on-foreigners-from-holdings-of-foreign-securities .  Preliminary data were released and posted on the Treasury web site on August 31, 2025. The survey was undertaken jointly by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. A complementary survey measuring foreign portfolio holdings of U.S. securities also occurs annually.  Data from the most recent such survey, for securities held at end-June 2026, are currently being processed.  Preliminary results are expected to be reported on February 26, 2027. Overall Results This survey measured the value of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 as approximately $19.3 trillion, with $15.2 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.6 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities (original term-to-maturity in excess of one year), and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The previous such survey, conducted as of year-end 2024, measured U.S. holdings of approximately $15.8 trillion, with $12.1 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.3 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities, and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The increase in U.S. holdings of foreign securities in 2025 was mainly in equity (see Table 1). U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities by country at the end of 2025 were the largest for the Cayman Islands ($3.1 trillion), followed by the United Kingdom ($2.0 trillion), Canada ($1.9 trillion), and Japan ($1.5 trillion) (see Table 2). title: Remarks by Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent on New Fraud Prevention Measures in Minnesota
body: October 30, 2026 As prepared for delivery. ST. CLOUD, Minn .—Good afternoon.  Thank you all for being here today.  I am pleased to be joined by FBI Director Kash Patel, CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, and Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald as we bring new force to the fight against fraud. President Trump has made clear that the war on fraud is not the work of one department, but a mandate we must carry across the Administration.  I am proud to stand alongside so many dedicated colleagues who are delivering on that mandate every day. America is a generous country.  And the compassion of our people imposes a corresponding duty on our government. That is why I visited Minnesota in January to make clear that the U.S. Treasury is deploying every tool to bring an end to this egregious, unchecked fraud and hold perpetrators to account. Over the past year, Treasury returned $175 million in payments that would have gone to deceased individuals—and expanded Do Not Pay access from 4 to 99 percent of federal programs. Further, we’ve stopped almost $190 million and returned over $100 million in funds to U.S. victims of overseas fraud; ordered an audit of approximately $9 billion in Treasury contracts; and, together with our partners at the IRS, proposed stronger eligibility checks for health insurance tax credits. These actions form one front of a whole-of-government effort led by Vice President Vance.  The Vice President’s task force first convened in March.  And he has worked tirelessly to restore vigilance and responsible stewardship in the management of public money. Since January 2025, the Trump Administration has uncovered more than $260 billion in fraud, prevented $72 billion in taxpayer funds from going out the door to illicit actors annually, and brought enforcement actions involving nearly $60 billion. Nowhere is this work more urgent than here in Minnesota. In the weeks following my visit, Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, known as FinCEN, issued a Geographic Targeting Order to trace criminal networks that divert funds overseas—and ensure that taxpayer dollars go to the American people, not terror groups like al-Shabaab.  We have ongoing investigations at home and abroad into al-Shabaab, its network and its enablers. Since the start of the Trump Administration, FinCEN data have also supported the law enforcement effort that led to the arrest and charging of 115 fraudsters, as well as seventy-five convictions and nearly 3,000 subpoenas across Minnesota. And just yesterday, IRS-CI assisted with investigative activity at several sites suspected of fraud.  I want to give a shoutout to our great officers at IRS-CI.  They don’t get much press, but they are quietly one of the most effective groups in the United States government for fighting fraud. Today, FinCEN released additional information to help refer new leads to law enforcement and provide support to ongoing investigations. We issued a notice to help financial institutions identify and report suspicious activity, especially involving charities and nonprofits. The notice highlights how criminals exploit fundraising capabilities to facilitate terrorist financing, fraud, and other illicit activity. FinCEN also issued an alert on the risks associated with cross-border transactions originated by money services businesses, known as MSBs. The alert details how bad actors can exploit MSBs to move funds overseas. FinCEN identified over $8 billion in potentially suspicious foreign agent-directed payments between 2021 and 2025 alone. And today’s alert urges financial institutions to be vigilant in detecting, identifying, and reporting suspicious activity arising from certain cross-border payments involving U.S.-based MSBs. The next phase of this fight, meanwhile, will make it easier than ever for whistleblowers who know where fraud is hiding to lead us to it. Until now, any citizen who detected fraud was forced to navigate a maze of tip lines scattered across law enforcement agencies. No more. For the first time, we’ve created a single, centralized portal at America.gov/fraud. Treasury is proud to seed this new, $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program. And anyone who submits information that leads to a conviction or enforcement action may be eligible for a reward up to $30,000. Speaking up has long carried a cost for whistleblowers. Under President Trump, it can offer a reward. Now, the industrial-scale fraud that Tim Walz shamefully, and perhaps knowingly, allowed to fester is the defining legacy of his administration. But with President Trump back in office, Washington is no longer content to watch Minnesota’s fraud epidemic spiral from a distance. The days of indifference are over. And under this President’s leadership, wherever the money leads, the full weight of government will follow. Now, I am pleased to turn it over to someone who has helped to give the fight against fraud both its discipline and its force, FBI Director Kash Patel. ###

title: October 30, 2026 - FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Groundbreaking therapy provides additional treatment option that fights the disease at its source, not only its symptoms For Immediate Release: October 30, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options. “Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) . “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.” The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit. RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11).  Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells. The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment. The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site. The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

title: ICYMI: Secretary Bessent, Trump Administration Officials Announce New Fraud Prevention Measures in Minnesota
body: October 30, 2026 ST. CLOUD, Minn.— Today, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent traveled to St. Cloud, Minnesota, along with Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Chairman Andrew Ferguson, and Assistant Attorney General for the National Fraud Enforcement Division Colin McDonald, to announce several initiatives to combat the rampant fraud that has wasted billions of taxpayer dollars in Minnesota. Today’s announcements underscore the Trump Administration’s coordinated efforts to protect taxpayer dollars, prevent fraud, and hold perpetrators accountable. Yesterday, FBI Minneapolis executed numerous search warrants related to ongoing fraud investigations in a combined 26- count indictment, and arrested four alleged Medicaid fraudsters who intended to defraud victims of over $41 million with actual losses amounting to $21.65 million . This was the outcome of an investigation by the FBI, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and Homeland Security Investigations. To further strengthen fraud prevention and detection, Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) today issued an alert on risks involving cross-border payments through U.S.-based money services businesses after financial institutions reported more than $8 billion in potentially suspicious wire payments from 2021 to 2025. FinCEN also issued a notice to help financial institutions detect and report the exploitation of charities and nonprofits for terrorist financing, fraud, and other illicit activity. “President Trump has made clear that the war on fraud is not the work of one department, but a mandate we must carry across the Administration,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent . “The U.S. Treasury is deploying every tool to bring an end to this egregious, unchecked fraud and hold perpetrators to account. And under this President’s leadership, wherever the money leads, the full weight of the federal government will follow.” Read Secretary Bessent’s op-ed in the Minnesota Star-Tribune . “Our nation’s War on Fraud began in the Medicaid program right here in Minnesota. Since then, we’ve embarked on an unprecedented quest to crush corruption here and nationwide,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz . “No society, no American, no patient should ever be the victim of the crimes we’ve seen since then. Fraudsters aren’t just stealing taxpayer dollars. they are threatening the quality, affordability, and integrity of the healthcare millions of Americans rely on.” “We’re identifying criminal funding streams, locating their center of gravity, and dismantling their networks across the country. That includes crushing the criminal fraud complex that has plagued America for so long,” said FBI Director Kash Patel . “The FBI is following the money, and if you steal from the government or American taxpayers, justice will find you." “States such as Minnesota got a free pass for four full years. During this time, criminals were allowed to steal money from hardworking Americans and live a life of luxury while everyone else suffered,” said FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson . “President Trump, Vice President Vance, and Secretary Bessent had a very clear message: Enough is enough. The era of robbing American citizens is over. We are putting Americans first again.” “Minnesota is the epicenter for fraud in America,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter for the Justice Department . “The Trump administration’s crackdown is working, and the results speak for themselves. Through the Minnesota Fraud Task Force we are systematically dismantling schemes preying on Americans. Backed by more than a thousand subpoenas and 40 warrants, the message is simple: No one stealing from taxpayer-funded programs is safe.” “The alarming concentration of fraud targeting taxpayer-funded programs in Minnesota demands a coordinated and sustained response,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division . “We are working with our law enforcement partners to uncover alleged fraud, protect public funds, and hold offenders accountable. We will continue these efforts until these schemes are dismantled and taxpayer dollars are protected from abuse in Minnesota.” The full press conference is available to watch here . Read more about Treasury’s announced fraud prevention measures . ###
